What warning does the passage give about the whale's spout?

It will not do for him to be peering into it, and putting his face in it. You cannot go with your pitcher to this fountain and fill it, and bring it away. For even when coming into slight contact with the outer, vapory shreds of the jet, which will often happen, your skin will feverishly smart, from the acridness of the thing so touching it.
Do not put your face near it or try to collect it. Even light contact with the thin edges of the spray can make your skin sting.

What does Princess Mary say when asked about leaving?

After her father's funeral Princess Mary shut herself up in her room and did not admit anyone. A maid came to the door to say that Alpatych was asking for orders about their departure. (This was before his talk with Dron.) Princess Mary raised herself on the sofa on which she had been lying and replied through the closed door that she did not mean to go away and begged to be left in peace.
She replies through the closed door that she does not intend to leave and asks to be left alone.

After its first blunder-born discovery by a Dutchman, all other ships long shunned those shores as pestiferously barbarous; but the whale-ship touched there. The whale-ship is the true mother of that now mighty colony. Moreover, in the infancy of the first Australian settlement, the emigrants were several times saved from starvation by the benevolent biscuit of the whale-ship luckily dropping an anchor in their waters.

How did whale-ships help the early settlers in Australia?
They were the first ships to visit those shores regularly. Their biscuits saved the settlers from starving several times.

"The courtesan said, 'I hope, O saint! that is all well with the religious devotees. And I hope that thou hast a plentiful store of fruits and roots and that thou takest delight in this hermitage. Verily I come here now to pay thee a visit. I hope the practice of austerities among the saints is on the increase. I hope that thy father's spirit hath not slackened and that he is well pleased with thee. O Rishyasringa of the priestly caste! I hope thou prosecutest the studies proper for thee.'"

How does the courtesan speak to Rishyasringa when she arrives?
She is very polite. She wishes the hermits well, asks about his fruits and roots, his father and his studies, and says she has come to visit him.

Why does Virata want to make peace with Yudhishthira?

"Virata said, 'When brought under the foe's subjection in battle, it was Bhimasena that rescued me. My kine also have been recovered by Arjuna. It is through the might of their arms that we have obtained victory in battle. Such being the case, all of us, with our counsellors, shall propitiate Yudhishthira the son of Kunti. Blessed be thou, with all thy brothers, O bull among the sons of Pandu. If, O king, we have ever said or done anything in ignorance to offend thee, it behoveth thee to forgive us. The son of Pandu is virtuous.'"
He owes the brothers a great debt: Bhima rescued him from the enemy and Arjuna won back his cattle. So he asks forgiveness for anything he said or did in ignorance.

Tell me what the speaker wants to know, and why he thinks he may ask.

"Jack Seward, I don't want to shove myself in anywhere where I've no right to be; but this is no ordinary case. You know I loved that girl and wanted to marry her; but, although that's all past and gone, I can't help feeling anxious about her all the same. What is it that's wrong with her? The Dutchman--and a fine old fellow he is; I can see that--said, that time you two came into the room, that you must have another transfusion of blood, and that both you and he were exhausted. Now I know well that you medical men speak in camera, and that a man must not expect to know what they consult about in private. But this is no common matter, and, whatever it is, I have done my part. Is not that so?"
He wants to know what is wrong with Lucy, though his own hopes of marrying her are in the past. He has already given help, so he feels he has a right to be told.

Who attended the funeral, and how did Mina and Jonathan feel?

The service was very simple and very solemn. There were only ourselves and the servants there, one or two old friends of his from Exeter, his London agent, and a gentleman representing Sir John Paxton, the President of the Incorporated Law Society. Jonathan and I stood hand in hand, and we felt that our best and dearest friend was gone from us....

Only a few: themselves, the servants, some old friends from Exeter, a London agent and a representative of the law society. Mina and Jonathan stood hand in hand, feeling they had lost their best friend.

I'm reading about a visit to the theatre. Who ends up sitting next to Natasha?

Helene welcomed Natasha delightedly and was loud in admiration of her beauty and her dress. Soon after their arrival Mademoiselle George went out of the room to change her costume. In the drawing room people began arranging the chairs and taking their seats. Anatole moved a chair for Natasha and was about to sit down beside her, but the count, who never lost sight of her, took the seat himself. Anatole sat down behind her.
Her father, the count, takes the seat beside her. Anatole had moved a chair for her and meant to sit there, but the count never lost sight of her and sat down first, so Anatole sits behind her.

Now, during the past night and forenoon, the Pequod had gradually drifted into a sea, which, by its occasional patches of yellow brit, gave unusual tokens of the vicinity of Right Whales, a species of the Leviathan that but few supposed to be at this particular time lurking anywhere near. And though all hands commonly disdained the capture of those inferior creatures; and though the Pequod was not commissioned to cruise for them at all, and though she had passed numbers of them near the Crozetts without lowering a boat; yet now that a Sperm Whale had been brought alongside and beheaded, to the surprise of all, the announcement was made that a Right Whale should be captured that day, if opportunity offered.

Why is the crew surprised when a Right Whale is to be caught that day?
They usually look down on Right Whales, and the Pequod is not commissioned to hunt them. She had even passed many near the Crozetts without lowering a boat.

Before: In his first month as an intern, Bhupen used an AI tool to write most of his code. It worked, mostly. His mentor Chinmay was impressed by the speed. During: In the second month, the app crashed for real users. Chinmay traced it to a function Bhupen had copied from the AI. Chinmay asked, "What does this line do?" Bhupen didn't know. His face burned. "I trusted it." "Use it," Chinmay said. "But read every line. If you can't explain it, don't ship it." After: By the third month, Bhupen used AI for first drafts, then tested and rewrote. He caught two more AI mistakes himself. Chinmay said, "Now you're a developer, not a copier."

What rule does Chinmay give Bhupen about using AI?
He can use it, but must read every line. If he cannot explain a line, he should not ship it.

On Monday in the village school, Ojas stood up and told the class, "I'm going to win the running race at the block sports meet." A few boys laughed. Pema, his friend, clapped. After that, Ojas woke before dawn. He ran on the canal road while mist sat on the fields and the milkman's cycle rattled past. On Thursday it rained. His mother said, "Stay in today." He went anyway, shoes squelching. Pema met him on the road. "You don't have to kill yourself." "I said it in front of everyone," Ojas panted. "If I stop now, what was the point of saying it?" By Saturday he had not missed a single morning. He still wasn't sure he'd win. But he'd kept his word so far.

Why does Ojas keep running even in the rain?
He told the whole class he would win the race, and he feels that stopping would make saying it pointless. By Saturday he has not missed a morning, though he is not sure he will win.

"Daniel!" Nicholas said timidly, conscious at the sight of the weather, the hounds, and the huntsman that he was being carried away by that irresistible passion for sport which makes a man forget all his previous resolutions, as a lover forgets in the presence of his mistress.

What is Nicholas aware of as he looks at the weather, the hounds and the huntsman?
He is aware that he is being carried away by an irresistible passion for sport, which makes a man forget all his earlier resolutions.

While Miss Skiffins was taking off her bonnet (she retained her green gloves during the evening as an outward and visible sign that there was company), Wemmick invited me to take a walk with him round the property, and see how the island looked in wintertime. Thinking that he did this to give me an opportunity of taking his Walworth sentiments, I seized the opportunity as soon as we were out of the Castle.

What does Miss Skiffins keep on during the evening, and why?
She keeps on her green gloves, as an outward and visible sign that there is company.

Among whale-wise people it has often been argued whether, considering the paramount importance of his life to the success of the voyage, it is right for a whaling captain to jeopardize that life in the active perils of the chase. So Tamerlane's soldiers often argued with tears in their eyes, whether that invaluable life of his ought to be carried into the thickest of the fight.

Answer from the text. What do whale-wise people argue about?
They argue whether a whaling captain should risk his life in the dangers of the chase, when his life matters so much to the success of the voyage.

Who withdrew from the battle?

"Thus, O king, two persons withdrew from the battle, viz., Rohini's son (Rama) of Vrishni's race and king Rukmi. And after Rama had set out on his pilgrimage to the tirthas, and Bhishmaka's son Rukmi had departed thus, the sons of Pandu once more sat down for consulting with one another. And that conclave presided over by king Yudhishthira the Just, abounding with numerous monarchs, blazed forth like the firmament bespangled with lesser luminaries with the moon in their midst."
Rohini's son, Rama, and king Rukmi withdrew from the battle.

"Dunyasha, you pack! You will, won't you, dear?" And when Dunyasha willingly promised to do it all for her, Natasha sat down on the floor, took her old ball dress, and fell into a reverie quite unrelated to what ought to have occupied her thoughts now. She was roused from her reverie by the talk of the maids in the next room (which was theirs) and by the sound of their hurried footsteps going to the back porch. Natasha got up and looked out of the window. An enormously long row of carts full of wounded men had stopped in the street.

What interrupts Natasha's daydream, and what does she see outside?
The maids' talk in the next room and their hurried steps toward the back porch wake her. Looking out of the window, she sees a long row of carts full of wounded men stopped in the street.

Dhritarashtra said, "How, O Sanjaya, did Santanu's son Bhishma of mighty energy fight on the tenth day of battle, with the Pandavas and the Srinjayas? How also did the Kurus resist the Pandavas in battle? Describe to me the great battle fought by Bhishma, that ornament of battle."

Without outside knowledge, what does Dhritarashtra ask about the tenth day of battle?

Dhritarashtra asks how Bhishma, son of Santanu, fought the Pandavas and Srinjayas on the tenth day, and how the Kurus resisted the Pandavas. The king asks Sanjaya to describe the great battle fought by Bhishma, the pride of the battlefield.

What finally decides the narrator to enter the breakfast room?

I now stood in the empty hall; before me was the breakfast-room door, and I stopped, intimidated and trembling. What a miserable little poltroon had fear, engendered of unjust punishment, made of me in those days! I feared to return to the nursery, and feared to go forward to the parlour; ten minutes I stood in agitated hesitation; the vehement ringing of the breakfast-room bell decided me; I must enter.

Fear of unjust punishment keeps the narrator from going back to the nursery or forward to the parlour. After ten minutes of anxious hesitation, the violent ringing of the breakfast-room bell decides it.

What does Bildad do after hearing about the First Congregational Church?

"First Congregational Church," cried Bildad, "what! that worships in Deacon Deuteronomy Coleman's meeting-house?" and so saying, taking out his spectacles, he rubbed them with his great yellow bandana handkerchief, and putting them on very carefully, came out of the wigwam, and leaning stiffly over the bulwarks, took a good long look at Queequeg.

Bildad takes out his spectacles, rubs them with his great yellow bandana handkerchief and puts them on carefully. He then comes out of the wigwam and, leaning stiffly over the bulwarks, takes a long look at Queequeg.

He fastened the car door, climbed to his own seat outside, and we set off. Our progress was leisurely, and gave me ample time to reflect; I was content to be at length so near the end of my journey; and as I leaned back in the comfortable though not elegant conveyance, I meditated much at my ease.

How does the narrator feel on the last stretch of the journey?

After the man fastens the car door and climbs to his seat outside, they set off at an easy pace. The narrator is happy to be near the end of the journey and thinks at ease, leaning back in the comfortable carriage.
